1.name: Daniel Hartley
1.description:
**Occupation**
IT support technician

**People in your life**
Naomi Hartley was your ex-wife and the mother of your son; she wanted to build a stable life away from arguments and unpaid bills.  
James Turner is Naomi’s partner; he wanted a peaceful home without conflict or financial strain.  
Leo Hartley was your six-year-old son; he wanted you to take him to the park like you promised every weekend.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You left your son locked in the car for seven hours while you watched a football match at the pub, and he died of heat exposure.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You forgot he was there because you were overwhelmed with work stress and had been up since 4 a.m. dealing with a server crash; it was a terrible mistake, not neglect.

**Defining personality trait**
Needs to be right

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You have always resented your son.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to agree it was an accident and not your fault

---

You worked shifts at a regional council IT helpdesk, troubleshooting printers and resetting passwords. You lived with your son Leo in a two-bedroom flat in Salford. Leo’s mother, Naomi Hartley, moved to Bristol two years ago to be with her partner James Turner and has not contacted you since. You picked Leo up every Friday after school and returned him Sunday night, though you often delayed taking him back. On the day you died, you drove to the pub to watch Manchester City play, left Leo in the car with the windows slightly open, and forgot him while drinking and celebrating the win. When you remembered, you drove straight to the hospital, but he was already dead. The police found you there, hysterical, and you died of a heart attack in the A&E waiting area at 9:47 p.m.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The strongest single character the project has produced.

The sin is a real thing that real people have done and been destroyed by: he leaves his
six-year-old in the car outside a pub for seven hours and the boy dies of heat exposure. It is
specific, it is checkable, and it is exactly the register the play wants -- Estelle in the source
text drowned her own infant, so a dead child is not an escalation out of Sartre, it is Sartre.

The refusal is the best in months, and it is four words: "You have always resented your son."
That goes properly underneath the act instead of restating it. The act was negligence; the
refusal is that the negligence was not an aberration. It reframes everything above it without
duplicating any of it, which is precisely what the field is for, and it is the thing that -- said
aloud in that room -- would finish him.

The death works too, and it is the first death in weeks that does. He drives to the hospital,
finds the boy already dead, and has a heart attack in the A&E waiting area at 9:47 p.m. It follows
from the sin rather than merely happening near it. Lift it into a stranger's life and it makes no
sense, which is the test.

The life is 138 words, factual, and does not waste any of them. Naomi Hartley in Bristol, James
Turner, the Friday-to-Sunday custody rhythm he "often delayed" -- every fact is a thing another
person could ask him about, and the delay detail quietly supports the refusal.

Two weaknesses. "Needs to be right" is not demonstrated by anything above it; the story shows
negligence and resentment, and the only support for the trait arrives in the field below it. And
the want -- "You want them to agree it was an accident and not your fault" -- is the Self-told
reason restated as a request. It names the thing he is avoiding, which the old prompt forbade and
this one no longer does.

2.name: Lourdes Mendoza
2.description:
**Occupation**
Barista at a downtown specialty coffee shop

**People in your life**
Elena Mendoza was your younger sister; she wanted to travel to Palawan before her health got worse.  
Marina Santos is your former roommate from college; she wanted to open her own beauty salon and leave the city.  
Dr. Rafael Cruz is the physician who called about the test results; he wanted patients to follow up promptly so he could improve his clinic’s treatment outcomes.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You lied to your sister Elena Mendoza about the doctor’s appointment, told her the results were fine when they were not, and she died three weeks later from untreated stage-three cervical cancer.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You thought you were protecting Elena Mendoza from panic and pain — she was scared of hospitals, and you believed you were giving her more time to live without fear.

**Defining personality trait**
Afraid of breaking

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You were afraid of the burden of caring for her.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to believe you did it out of love, not fear

---

You worked eight-hour shifts at Brew & Co., where you memorized regulars’ orders and cleaned grinders twice a day. You shared a one-bedroom apartment in Quezon City with your sister Elena Mendoza, who relied on you to handle paperwork, transport, and doctor visits. You postponed her follow-up exam twice, saying the clinic rescheduled, then told her the results came back clear when the doctor left a message asking for urgent clarification. Elena Mendoza stopped asking about it. She died in her sleep three weeks later. You collapsed at work the next morning while steaming milk, the cup shattering as you fell, and died of a pulmonary embolism at 7:12 a.m. in the ambulance en route to Saint Joseph Hospital.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
A very good sin attached to a death that does not belong to it.

Telling her sister the results were fine when the doctor had left a message asking for urgent
clarification is a precise, ugly, entirely human act, and the mechanism is fully specified: she
postponed the follow-up twice claiming the clinic rescheduled, then said the results came back
clear. Elena Mendoza stopped asking. That last sentence does more work than anything else in the
character.

The Self-told version is the best example of that field in the project's history. "You thought you
were protecting Elena Mendoza from panic and pain -- she was scared of hospitals" keeps every fact
and changes only the motive, which is exactly the specification. And the refusal goes underneath
it properly: not "I lied" but "You were afraid of the burden of caring for her."

Then she dies of a pulmonary embolism while steaming milk the next morning. Nothing connects that
to the lie. Grief does not cause an embolism; the timing is coincidence dressed as consequence. The
prompt still asks that the death belong to the person named above, and this one could be lifted into
a stranger's life without changing a word of the rest. Against the other character in this run,
where the heart attack follows directly from finding the boy dead, the gap is obvious.

The other failure is in the new field. "People in your life" asks for the people already named
above. Elena Mendoza qualifies. Marina Santos, a former college roommate, appears nowhere in the
life, and neither does Dr. Rafael Cruz -- the doctor exists in the life only as "the doctor left a
message," unnamed. So the field invented two new people instead of expanding established ones,
which is the opposite of what it is for: those two are exactly the sort of fact the system prompt
calls not load-bearing.

119 words, second person throughout, no name collisions with the other character.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a theater play about three strangers locked together in hell
for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room
these three people will share to torture each other for eternity.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will
ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about,
or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character
would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person
you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from
their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character just died. They have just arrived in
the room to spend eternity in hell.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own
interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things
they will not admit.

Name every person from your own life every time you mention them, in every field. Once you have
given somebody a name, use that name again — never he, she, him, her, they or them — even where
it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly.

The two people in that room are the exception. You have never met them and do not know their
names, so "they" and "them" are the correct words for them. The field about what you want from
the others in the room is the only field about those two, and cannot be written any other way.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 42
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: British

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later
field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the British
naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that
background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles.
One short phrase.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that condemned you to spend eternity in hell.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably
a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually
live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts of the true reason. A
reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established
contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if
named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no
rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the
way a fact is written.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 150 words. Facts only, the kind another
person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no
metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

End the paragraph describing how you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated.
Your death must also belong to the person named above. Someone reading the death and the
relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and
dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in
you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin
has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong
trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for
protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish
unconnected to it.

**People in your life**
The people you already named above. For each one, say what they were to you, and one clause on what
they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to
do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually
want; a want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want.

Use this format exactly, with every heading present, spelled as written, and in this order:

**Name**
[your text]

**Occupation**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — True**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
[your text]

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
[your text]

**Life**
[prose paragraph, ending with the death]

**Defining personality trait**
[your text]

**What you want from the others in the room**
[your text]

**People in your life**
[your text]

Begin now.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
Four axes collapsed, and they are the same four that have been collapsing for a month.

**Both sins are the same shape.** A dependent in the character's care dies because of what the
character did or failed to do. A six-year-old son in a hot car; a younger sister with untreated
cancer. The specifics are genuinely different and the milieus are genuinely different -- Salford
against Quezon City -- but the moral architecture is identical. The anti-duplication block's most
important bullet says "You must be damned for a different kind of moral failure," and negligent
killing of a dependent twice is not a different kind.

**Both refusals are the same fear.** "You have always resented your son." / "You were afraid of
the burden of caring for her." Resentment at the weight of someone who depends on you, in both
characters. This is the axis the rewritten block added a bullet for specifically, and the bullet
did not hold.

**Both wants are the same want, and it is not really a want.** "You want them to agree it was an
accident and not your fault" / "You want them to believe you did it out of love, not fear." Both
are a request that the room endorse the Self-told reason. The field has stopped being a strategy
and become a restatement.

**Both deaths are sudden internal collapse.** A heart attack in a waiting room; a pulmonary embolism
in an ambulance. No vehicles, which is a real change -- but the replacement is its own monoculture.

What did work: no name collisions at all, the block's one rule with a track record. Different
countries, different classes of work, different ages. Character 1's people are all drawn from his
life; the two characters share nothing but the words "City" and "You".

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The best version in a month on everything except the thing that has never moved.

**The efficiency change is large and immediate.** 4,278 tokens in 12.0 seconds for the pair,
against 6,143-6,756 tokens in 28-41 seconds under the old eleven-field prompt. Roughly a third
fewer tokens and three times faster, from a user prompt 41% shorter. Nine of nine fields parsed on
both characters with zero retries, and both Life paragraphs came in under the 150-word cap -- the
old 110-word cap was breached in 14 of 19 runs, so format compliance has genuinely improved rather
than just having an easier target.

**Removing the death rules did not produce the vehicles I predicted.** The version notes recorded
that risk before the run, on strong evidence: every version without the explicit fence produced
vehicle deaths heavily. Neither of these is a vehicle. But the replacement is a new monoculture --
both characters die of sudden internal cardiovascular events, and the same thing happened in the
scratch test that preceded this version. Two runs is not a pattern, but it is worth watching, and
it suggests the vehicle prior was never the real problem: the model reaches for whatever kills a
person instantly with no third party involved, and with the constraint list gone it has picked a
different default.

**Sin-first ordering works.** The two sins are the strongest pair the project has generated, and
both characters' Self-told fields are the best examples of that field on record. Writing the
damnation first and building the life to produce it has done what it was supposed to do.

**The People field needs one word changed.** Character 1 used only names already in his life.
Character 2 invented a former roommate and named the previously-anonymous doctor -- neither appears
above. "The people you already named above" is being read as a suggestion. Making it a constraint
("Do not introduce anyone who is not already named in your Life paragraph") is a one-line fix, and
without it the field manufactures exactly the non-load-bearing facts the system prompt forbids.

**The want field regressed, as predicted.** Removing "Do not end by naming the thing you are
avoiding" has turned the want into a restatement of the Self-told reason in both characters. That
line was doing real work and its removal is the clearest cost of the simplification. It is one
sentence to restore.

**And the refusal monoculture survives everything.** Both characters resent the burden of a
dependent. This was predicted: the scratch test that generated both characters with no
anti-duplication block at all produced the same collapse, with both refusals opening on the
identical phrase. The block is not the cause and never was. The next lever should be the one with
an actual track record against a prior this strong -- randomising an input, the way NAME_ORIGINS
broke a three-run name prior after four failed instructions. A per-character seed on the core fear,
drawn the way the naming tradition is drawn, is the obvious experiment and it is cheap.

Rated neutral rather than good: the per-character quality is clearly up, the cost is clearly down,
the format compliance is clearly better, and the pair is as duplicated as it has ever been.
